title: Tracking Your Spending
description: Find out where your money really goes, not where you think it goes.
wolfLine: You can’t fix what you won’t look at.

tracking.definition: Writing down what you actually spend, so you can compare it with your budget.
tracking.example: Checking your bank app at the end of each week and noting what went where.

budget-leak.definition: Money that slips away on things you barely notice or don't really use.
budget-leak.example: A subscription you forgot about, or daily snacks that add up.

spending-category.definition: A bucket you group purchases into, like housing, food, transport or fun, so you can see totals.
spending-category.example: Groceries, lunch at work and coffee all go in “Food.”

transaction.definition: One movement of money: a purchase, a payment or a deposit, with a date and an amount.

envelope-method.definition: Budgeting with cash: each category gets its own envelope, and when it’s empty, that category is done for the month.
envelope-method.example: Put $200 in a “Food” envelope. Spend it, and food is done until next month.

emotional-spending.definition: Buying things to change how you feel (bored, stressed, sad or celebrating) rather than because you planned to.
emotional-spending.example: Ordering clothes at midnight after a terrible day.

lessons.title: Track the Leaks
lessons.summary: Find where the money actually goes.

steps.context: A budget is the plan. [[Tracking]] is checking what you actually spent, so you can see whether you stuck to it.
steps.prompt: Why track your spending?
choices: To see where your money really goes
steps.explain: Most people guess low. Tracking shows the truth.

steps.context: Small habits add up. A $3 snack every workday, about 20 days a month, costs $3 × 20 = $60 a month.
steps.prompt: A coffee costs $5. You buy one every workday, about 20 days a month. What's that per month?
At $100 a month, what does that coffee habit cost over a year (12 months)?
steps.explain: $100 × 12 = $1,200. Small habit, big number.

steps.context: A [[budget leak]] is money that slips away on things you barely notice or don't really use.
steps.prompt: Which of these is most likely a budget leak?
choices: A subscription you forgot you're paying for
steps.explain: Paying every month for something you don't use. Cancel it.

steps.prompt: Small purchases don't matter as long as each one is cheap.
steps.explain: Ten small buys a week is one big buy a month.

steps.prompt: Tracking shows you spent $300 on takeout last month. What's the smart move?
choices: Stop tracking so you don't feel bad
Set a takeout limit in next month's budget
steps.explain: Tracking finds the leak. The budget plugs it.

lessons.title: Spending Categories
lessons.summary: Put every purchase in a bucket so you can see the pattern.

steps.context: To see where money goes, group each purchase into a [[spending category]]: housing, food, transport, fun and so on.
steps.prompt: Which category does a bus ticket belong in?
steps.explain: Getting around is transport.

steps.prompt: Sort last week’s spending into categories.
Which set of categories is easiest to stick with?
choices: Housing, food, transport, fun, saving, other
A separate category for every store
steps.explain: Five to eight categories is plenty. Too many and you’ll stop tracking.

steps.context: What matters is the total in each bucket. Add up everything in one category.
steps.prompt: Food this week: groceries $64, lunch $12, coffee $9, more groceries $38. What’s the food total?
If every week looks like that, about how much goes on food in a month? Use 4 weeks.
A coffee bought on the way to work belongs in the transport category.
steps.explain: It’s food. Where you bought it doesn’t change what it is.

steps.prompt: What’s the point of categories?
choices: To see which kind of spending is biggest
To spend more in each one
steps.explain: Totals by category show you where to look first.

lessons.title: Read Your Spending Log
lessons.summary: One week of real transactions. Find the pattern.

steps.context: Every purchase is a [[transaction]]: one line with a date, a name and an amount.
steps.prompt: How many transactions happened on Oct 2?
steps.explain: City Grocer and the gas station.

steps.prompt: How much went on groceries this week?
Not counting rent, how much was spent this week?
After rent, which category was biggest this week?
How much did fun cost: the streaming service and the movie?
One week of transactions is enough to plan a whole year.
steps.explain: One week is a snapshot. Track a full month to see the real pattern.

lessons.title: Ways to Track
lessons.summary: App, spreadsheet, envelopes or a notebook: pick the one you’ll keep.

steps.title: Pick a method you’ll keep
steps.body:
There’s no single right way to track. What matters is doing it every week.

**Bank app:** already lists every card payment. **Budgeting app:** sorts transactions into categories for you. **Spreadsheet:** you type them in and see totals. **Notebook:** old school, and it works.

steps.context: The [[envelope method]] is an old trick: cash for each category goes in its own envelope. When an envelope is empty, that category is done for the month.
steps.prompt: Your fun envelope is empty on the 22nd. What does the envelope method say?
choices: No more fun spending until next month
Take money from the rent envelope
steps.explain: An empty envelope means that category is done. That’s the whole point.

steps.prompt: Cash purchases still need tracking, even though they don’t show up in your bank app.
steps.explain: Cash leaves no trail unless you write it down.

steps.prompt: How often should you check your spending?
choices: Only when your account is empty
steps.explain: Weekly is often enough to catch problems, and rare enough to stick with.

steps.prompt: Match each method to what it’s best at.
Which tracking method is best?
choices: The one you’ll actually keep using
steps.explain: A simple method you use beats a perfect one you abandon.

lessons.title: Where It Went Over
lessons.summary: Compare the month with the plan and find what broke it.

steps.context: Tracking pays off when you compare it with your plan. Each line shows what you planned, and the amount is what you actually spent.
steps.prompt: Tap the category that went way over its plan.
steps.explain: Eating out: $260 spent against $120 planned.

steps.prompt: By how much did eating out go over?
The plan for all five categories added up to $1,840. How far over was the whole month?
What’s the most useful next step?
choices: Find out why eating out ran over, then set a realistic limit
Spend less on groceries to make up for it
why: The budget did its job: it showed you the leak.
Groceries were already under plan, and they’re a need.
steps.explain: The budget just showed you something useful. Use it.

steps.prompt: The money left over in groceries, transport and fun can cover part of the overspend.
steps.explain: $10 + $10 + $5 = $25 under plan. Moving it helps, but it doesn’t cover $140.

lessons.title: Riley’s Receipts
lessons.summary: A month of receipts tells a story. Add it up.

story.title: The receipt shoebox
story.body:
Riley kept every receipt in a shoebox for a month, then added them up on a Sunday night.

The big ones were no surprise: **$1,050** rent and **$340** groceries. The surprise was everything else: **22** coffees at **$5** each, **9** takeout dinners at about **$18**, and **$64** of apps and games Riley barely remembered buying.

Riley takes home **$2,500** a month and had been wondering why there was never anything left.

steps.prompt: How much did the coffees cost?
And the takeout dinners?
Add up coffee, takeout and the apps.
Now add rent and groceries. What was the shoebox total for the month?
Riley takes home $2,500 but the receipts only add to $1,726. What’s the most likely reason nothing is left?
choices: Some spending never made it into the shoebox
steps.explain: $774 is missing. Card taps, bills that pay themselves and cash rarely all come with receipts. That’s why tracking in a bank app helps.

steps.prompt: Riley wants to free up $150 a month. Which plan does it?
choices: Cut takeout to 2 dinners and coffee to 10 cups
steps.explain: 7 fewer dinners × $18 = $126, plus 12 fewer coffees × $5 = $60. That’s $186 a month.

lessons.title: Spotting Patterns
lessons.summary: Payday splurges, weekend leaks, bad-day buys.

steps.context: Look past single purchases to patterns: when, where and why you spend.
steps.prompt: Most of your spending happens in the three days after payday. What’s that?
steps.explain: Money feels endless right after payday. It isn’t.

steps.context: [[Emotional spending]] means buying to change how you feel: bored, stressed, sad, or celebrating.
steps.prompt: Which is most likely emotional spending?
choices: Ordering $60 of clothes at midnight after a terrible day
steps.explain: A bad day, a late hour, an unplanned buy: classic emotional spending.

steps.prompt: Noticing what triggers your spending makes it easier to change.
steps.explain: Once you know the trigger, you can plan around it.

steps.prompt: You spend about $45 every Saturday on things you didn’t plan. What’s that over a year of 52 Saturdays?
What’s a good fix for a payday splurge?
choices: Move savings out on payday, before you can spend it
steps.explain: If it’s gone before the splurge starts, there’s less to splurge.

steps.prompt: Planned or emotional? Sort them.
items: Retail therapy after a bad exam
Buying something because you were bored

lessons.title: The Monthly Check-In
lessons.summary: Fifteen minutes that steer next month.

steps.title: Fifteen minutes, once a month
steps.body: At the end of each month, sit down with your tracking and your budget. Compare, adjust, and set up next month. Fifteen minutes is enough.

steps.prompt: Put the monthly check-in in order.
items: Compare each category with the plan
Work out why anything ran over
steps.explain: Total, compare, understand, plan.

steps.prompt: You came in $60 under budget this month. What’s a good use of it?
choices: Give it a job, like savings or a goal
Let it sit and quietly disappear
Spend it fast before it’s gone
steps.explain: Money without a job wanders off. Give it one.

steps.prompt: If a category is under budget three months in a row, you can shrink it and move the money somewhere useful.
steps.explain: Your plan should match real life. Free that money up.

steps.context: Compare months to see whether you’re improving.
steps.prompt: Eating out was $310 in September and $240 in October. How much less did you spend?
If you keep October’s level, how much do you save over 12 months compared with September’s?
What’s the real goal of tracking?
steps.explain: Tracking looks back so you can plan forward.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Tracking
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: Your food spending for four weeks was $88, $102, $95 and $115. What’s the total for the month?
Which habit catches spending problems early?
steps.explain: Weekly checks catch a leak before it becomes a flood.

steps.prompt: The envelope method works by limiting each category to the cash in its envelope.
steps.explain: Empty envelope, category done.

steps.prompt: Your transport plan was $150 and you spent $190. What’s the honest next move?
choices: Find out why, then adjust the plan
steps.explain: Either the plan was too low or something changed. Find out which.
